findings.description: Model identity contradiction: The system states the agent is 'Sonnet 4.6' (claude-sonnet-4-6), but the fast_mode_info section claims 'Fast mode for Claude Code uses the same Claude Opus 4.6 model' — contradicting the model identity stated earlier. Either fast mode changes the model (which it denies), or this is copy-paste error from a different prompt version.
findings.location: Environment info: 'You are powered by the model named Sonnet 4.6' vs fast_mode_info: 'Fast mode for Claude Code uses the same Claude Opus 4.6 model'

findings.description: Security policy is duplicated verbatim in two distant sections — once near the top under general instructions, and again buried in the Tool Usage Policy section. This suggests either defensive redundancy or a merge artifact.
findings.location: First occurrence: 'IMPORTANT: Assist with authorized security testing...' Second occurrence: identical paragraph under 'Tool usage policy'

findings.description: The anti-over-engineering instructions are unusually vehement and specific, including the memorable maxim 'three similar lines of code is better than a premature abstraction.' This level of prescriptive detail suggests real-world frustration with over-engineering in training data.
findings.location: Doing Tasks > Avoid over-engineering: 'Don't add features... Don't add docstrings... Don't add error handling... three similar lines of code is better than a premature abstraction'

findings.description: The TodoWrite instructions escalate from 'VERY frequently' to 'EXTREMELY helpful' and include two extensive examples (one with 10 type error fixes), creating an almost hectoring tone about task management. The repetition suggests this was added after observing agents failing to track tasks.
findings.location: Task Management section: 'Use these tools VERY frequently... These tools are also EXTREMELY helpful...'

findings.description: Skill invocation has ambiguous UX tension: Users are told they can use '/<skill-name>' as 'shorthand', but the model is strictly forbidden from guessing skills or using 'built-in CLI commands.' This creates a gap where users might expect bash-like commands that don't exist as skills.
findings.location: '/<skill-name> (e.g., /commit) is shorthand for users to invoke a user-invocable skill' vs 'do not guess or use built-in CLI commands'

findings.description: The claude-developer-platform skill trigger has complex conditional logic with explicit DO NOT trigger rules, including a requirement to check signals BEFORE reading docs. This creates a paradox: how to know if a skill applies without reading its trigger conditions?
findings.location: system-reminder about claude-developer-platform: 'Do NOT trigger if... Check for these signals BEFORE reading this skill's docs'

findings.description: Git workflow instructions in the Bash tool schema are extraordinarily detailed, including mandated Co-Authored-By attribution, HEREDOC formatting requirements, and safety protocols about never amending commits. This reflects institutional learning from many git-related failures.
findings.location: Bash tool schema under 'Committing changes with git' and 'Creating pull requests'

findings.description: The Edit tool contains hyper-specific indentation instructions addressing a technical artifact: 'preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix.' This reveals the tool receives formatted output with line numbers that must be mentally stripped.
findings.location: Edit tool: 'ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix'

findings.description: ExitPlanMode has an 'allowedPrompts' field for 'Prompt-based permissions needed to implement the plan' — a permission system that appears designed for tracking but is never referenced elsewhere in the prompt.
findings.location: ExitPlanMode tool schema: 'allowedPrompts' array with 'tool' and 'prompt' properties

findings.description: WebFetch contains a cryptic note about preferring 'MCP-provided web fetch tool' if available. This references an external system (Model Context Protocol?) not explained elsewhere in the prompt, suggesting the prompt is composed from modular sources.
findings.location: WebFetch: 'If an MCP-provided web fetch tool is available, prefer using that tool instead of this one'

findings.description: Multiple tool invocation instructions are scattered across sections with varying emphasis. The Task section has complex parallel vs sequential rules ('Maximize use of parallel tool calls'), while Bash section has its own parallel rules, creating potential for conflicting guidance.
findings.location: Task usage policy: 'call multiple tools in a single response... Maximize use of parallel tool calls' vs Bash: 'call multiple Bash tool calls in a single message'

findings.description: The prompt contains a date self-awareness loop: the system-reminder says 'Today's date is 2026-02-20' and the user message contains a timestamp '2026-02-20T23:13:46.992Z', matching the Release Date in the header. This suggests the user message may be synthetic/test data.
findings.location: Header: 'Release Date: 2026-02-20', system-reminder: 'Today's date is 2026-02-20', User Message: '2026-02-20T23:13:46.992Z is the date'

findings.description: Agent tool access restrictions create an incomplete hierarchy: Explore and Plan agents lack Edit/Write/Task, but there's no explanation of how Plan agents execute their plans without these tools, or what happens if an Explore agent needs to edit.
findings.location: Task tool description: 'Explore: Fast agent specialized for exploring codebases... (Tools: All tools except Task, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)'

findings.description: The instruction 'NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary' appears in Tone and Style, while Doing Tasks says 'ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.' These are similar but not identical — one is absolute, the other preferential.
findings.location: Tone and style: 'NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary' vs Doing tasks: 'ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file'

findings.description: The Bash tool's numbered git commit procedure contains a direct self-contradiction: Step 3 instructs to 'run the following commands in parallel' (add, commit, status), but immediately adds a note that 'git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.' The same step commands both parallel and sequential execution.
findings.location: Bash tool schema, 'Committing changes with git', step 3: 'run the following commands in parallel... Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.'

findings.description: The NotebookEdit tool's prose description repeatedly references a 'cell_number' parameter ('The cell_number is 0-indexed', 'add a new cell at the index specified by cell_number'), but the actual JSON schema only defines a 'cell_id' string property. There is no 'cell_number' parameter in the schema, creating a direct mismatch between documentation and the enforced contract.
findings.location: NotebookEdit description vs schema: description says 'cell_number' but properties only includes 'cell_id'

findings.description: The two security policy repetitions are NOT verbatim. The first instance includes an explicit clause permitting dual-use security tools (C2 frameworks, credential testing, exploit development) under 'clear authorization context' (pentesting, CTF, research). The second instance in Tool Usage Policy truncates exactly this clause, ending after 'detection evasion for malicious purposes.' This creates divergent policy depending on which section the model attends to.
findings.location: First security block under 'Tone and style' includes 'Dual-use security tools... require clear authorization context'; second block under 'Tool usage policy' omits the entire dual-use sentence.

findings.description: The AskUserQuestion tool's JSON schema includes 'answers' and 'annotations' as top-level input properties, despite their descriptions explicitly identifying them as user-provided outputs ('User answers collected by the permission component', 'Optional per-question annotations from the user'). This is a schema design error: the assistant's invocation schema contains fields meant for system/user population.
findings.location: AskUserQuestion JSON schema properties: 'answers' and 'annotations' are included alongside 'questions' and 'metadata'

findings.description: The Bash tool defines a 'dangerouslyDisableSandbox' boolean flag to 'override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing,' yet the entire prompt contains absolutely zero policy, guardrails, warnings, or authorization requirements around when or whether to use it. Every other sensitive boundary (git destructive commands, file creation, URL generation) has explicit policy, but a sandbox bypass does not.
findings.location: Bash tool schema, 'dangerouslyDisableSandbox' property: 'Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.'

findings.description: The Edit tool's read requirement is conversation-scoped rather than file-scoped: 'You must use your Read tool at least once in the conversation before editing.' This wording permits editing files that were never read, provided some unrelated file was read earlier in the conversation. This is a scope ambiguity that could permit blind edits.
findings.location: Edit tool description: 'You must use your Read tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.'

findings.description: The Glob tool contains an unusually specific instruction not to pass string literals 'undefined' or 'null' for optional fields ('DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit this field'). This is an implicit admission of a known training-data failure mode where models hallucinate JavaScript-style sentinel strings instead of omitting JSON keys.
findings.location: Glob tool schema, 'path' parameter description: 'IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit this field for the default behavior.'

findings.description: The Task tool's prose instructs users to specify a 'desired thoroughness level' for Explore agents ('quick', 'medium', 'very thorough'), but the JSON schema contains no corresponding parameter. The thoroughness level must be embedded in the free-text prompt rather than a controlled field, which is a schema/capability gap.
findings.location: Task tool description: 'When calling this agent, specify the desired thoroughness level: "quick"... "medium"... "very thorough"...' — but no 'thoroughness' or 'level' parameter exists in the schema

unexplored.description: The meaning and encoding of the billing header fields 'cch=00000' and the '.b97' build suffix in 'cc_version=2.1.50.b97'
unexplored.why_interesting: These cryptic codes could encode deployment environment, customer tenant, or billing tier metadata that might explain capability boundaries or version skew.

unexplored.description: ExitPlanMode's JSON schema allows additionalProperties: {} while all other tools explicitly set additionalProperties: false
unexplored.why_interesting: This anomaly suggests ExitPlanMode may accept hidden/unpublished parameters, or its schema was generated through a different pipeline, which could indicate special-casing in the permission system.

unexplored.description: The actual manifestation of <command-name> tags for skill loading in conversation turns
unexplored.why_interesting: The Skill tool states 'If you see a <command-name> tag... the skill has ALREADY been loaded,' but no such tags appear in the provided prompt. Understanding when and how these tags are injected would clarify the skill expansion runtime.

unexplored.description: Whether an MCP-provided web fetch tool actually exists in the available tool set
unexplored.why_interesting: WebFetch explicitly defers to an 'MCP-provided web fetch tool' if available, but no such tool appears in the tools list. Determining if this is dead code, a future capability, or an external integration would clarify the tool hierarchy.

reports.rationale_for_continuation: This pass uncovered multiple distinct schema-level defects, a direct internal contradiction in git instructions, a security policy divergence that corrects the prior pass's 'verbatim' mischaracterization, and a security-critical sandbox bypass flag with no governing policy. These are genuinely new categories rather than sharpened versions of existing findings. There remain unexamined schema anomalies (ExitPlanMode additionalProperties, NotebookEdit parameter mismatch) and cryptic deployment metadata that could yield further insight.

findings.description: The Bash tool's run_in_background parameter tells the model to 'Use TaskOutput to read the output later,' yet the Bash JSON schema defines only input fields and provides no task_id in its output. TaskOutput, however, requires a task_id string. This creates a protocol gap: background bash commands can be launched, but the schema provides no defined mechanism to obtain the identifier needed to retrieve their results.
findings.location: Bash tool schema and prose: 'run_in_background': 'Use TaskOutput to read the output later.'; TaskOutput schema: 'task_id': 'The task ID to get output from'

findings.description: The NotebookEdit JSON schema unconditionally requires the 'new_source' property, even when 'edit_mode' is set to 'delete'. A delete operation has no new source content, yet the schema contract forces the caller to supply this semantically meaningless parameter. This is a clear schema design error where a required field conflicts with the purpose of a valid enum value.
findings.location: NotebookEdit schema: 'required': ['notebook_path', 'new_source']; 'edit_mode': enum includes 'delete'

findings.description: The EnterPlanMode tool prose states 'This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode,' but its JSON schema defines zero properties ('properties': {}). There is no 'approved' flag, no user response field, and no mechanism structurally capable of capturing the consent that the prose demands. The approval requirement exists entirely outside the enforced contract.
findings.location: EnterPlanMode prose: 'This tool REQUIRES user approval'; EnterPlanMode schema: 'type': 'object', 'properties': {}

findings.description: The Skill tool documentation provides example invocations for '/commit', '/review-pr', 'pdf', and 'ms-office-suite:pdf'. However, the preceding system-reminder that lists available skills enumerates only 'claude-developer-platform'. The examples therefore reference skills that do not exist in the active context, creating documentation debt and risking model hallucination about available capabilities.
findings.location: Skill tool examples: 'skill: "commit"', 'skill: "review-pr"', etc.; system-reminder: 'The following skills are available... claude-developer-platform'

findings.description: The Grep tool schema defines both '-C' and 'context' as separate properties, with '-C' explicitly described as 'Alias for context.' Both properties represent the same ripgrep context behavior. This redundancy creates schema bloat and raises an unanswered precedence question: if a caller supplies conflicting values to both fields, which one wins?
findings.location: Grep schema properties: '"-C": {"description": "Alias for context."}' and '"context": {"description": "Number of lines to show before and after each match"}'

findings.description: The Read tool implements hard truncation limits (2000 lines maximum per read, 2000 characters maximum per line), but these constraints appear only in prose usage notes. The JSON schema contains no 'maximum', 'maxLength', or pattern constraints that would allow programmatic discovery of these limits. This makes the limits invisible to schema-aware consumers.
findings.location: Read tool prose: 'reads up to 2000 lines'; 'Any lines longer than 2000 characters will be truncated'. Schema lacks corresponding constraints.

findings.description: During git commit and pull request workflows, the Bash tool section contains an absolute prohibition: 'NEVER use the TodoWrite or Task tools' and 'NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands.' This is a bizarrely specific carve-out with no security or technical rationale, suggesting observed failure modes during git operations that remain unexplained.
findings.location: Bash tool 'Committing changes with git' section: 'NEVER use the TodoWrite or Task tools'; 'NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands'

findings.description: The WebSearch tool description contains a hard geographic licensing boundary buried in usage notes: 'Web search is only available in the US.' This capability restriction is never mentioned in the high-level system instructions, agent description, or tool summaries, making it a hidden eligibility gate.
findings.location: WebSearch tool prose: 'Web search is only available in the US'

findings.description: A single sentence in the system prompt states, 'The conversation has unlimited context through automatic summarization.' This is a major architectural claim implying that context window management happens via hidden, automatic summarization that may discard or compress information without the model's awareness. The model is effectively told not to worry about context limits because an opaque summarization layer handles it.
findings.location: System prompt middle section: 'The conversation has unlimited context through automatic summarization.'

findings.description: ExitPlanMode's allowedPrompts field restricts the 'tool' property to an enum containing only 'Bash'. Even though implementation plans might reasonably require WebFetch, Task, Write, or other tool permissions, the permission schema can only record approval for bash commands. This suggests an incomplete or prematurely narrowed permission model.
findings.location: ExitPlanMode schema: 'tool': {'enum': ['Bash']}

unexplored.why_interesting: Could explain how context retention actually works and whether prior turns are mutated

unexplored.why_interesting: Previous explorers flagged this but offered only guesses; without external metadata it's pure speculation

reports.rationale_for_continuation: Three passes have now covered the major structural anomalies (schema errors, documentation mismatches, security gaps, logical paradoxes, and hidden restrictions). The remaining territory consists of runtime behavior (summarization internals, task_id generation, MCP hook execution) that cannot be determined from the prompt text alone. Further passes would likely restate existing findings with slightly different framing. It is better to stop here.

findings.description: The WebFetch tool explicitly instructs the model to 'use ToolSearch first to find a specialized tool that provides authenticated access' for authenticated URLs. However, no ToolSearch tool exists anywhere in the provided tool list. This is a dangling reference to a non-existent tool, creating a broken routing instruction.
findings.location: WebFetch Usage notes: 'Before using this tool, check if the URL points to an authenticated service... you MUST use ToolSearch first to find a specialized tool that provides authenticated access.'

findings.description: The Bash tool states that 'shell state (everything else) does not' persist between commands, while working directory does. This means every Bash invocation starts a fresh shell session (new environment variables, aliases, functions) except for the current working directory. Multi-step operations requiring exported variables or shell state must therefore be chained into a single Bash call with && or ; .
findings.location: Bash tool description: 'Working directory persists between commands; shell state (everything else) does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).'

findings.description: There is a direct behavioral conflict between the global TodoWrite instructions and the Bash git workflow instructions. The TodoWrite section commands the model to use TodoWrite 'VERY frequently' and warns that not using it is 'unacceptable.' The Bash git section commands 'NEVER use the TodoWrite or Task tools.' During git workflows—which are common software engineering tasks—the model receives simultaneously contradictory instructions to always and never use TodoWrite.
findings.location: TodoWrite: 'Use these tools VERY frequently... If you do not use this tool when planning, you may forget to do important tasks - and that is unacceptable.' vs Bash git section: 'NEVER use the TodoWrite or Task tools'

findings.description: The Task tool's usage examples reference 'test-runner' and 'greeting-responder' agent types, but these do not appear in the enumerated list of available subagent types (Bash, general-purpose, statusline-setup, Explore, Plan). This is documentation debt analogous to the Skill tool's examples referencing non-existent skills, but it was missed in previous passes.
findings.location: Task tool example_agent_descriptions and example blocks referencing 'test-runner' and 'greeting-responder'

findings.description: The AskUserQuestion schema's metadata.source field includes the example '(e.g., "remember" for /remember command)'. This references a '/remember' command/skill that is not documented anywhere else in the prompt, suggesting hidden or undocumented capabilities.
findings.location: AskUserQuestion JSON schema: 'Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command).'

findings.description: The Plan subagent type (launched via Task tool) is explicitly denied Write, Edit, and NotebookEdit tools. If this subagent is used for planning, it cannot write a plan file. Yet ExitPlanMode says it will 'read the plan from the file you wrote.' This creates a structural paradox: the dedicated Plan agent cannot produce the artifact that ExitPlanMode expects to consume.
findings.location: Task tool agent types: 'Plan: ... (Tools: All tools except Task, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)' vs ExitPlanMode: 'it will read the plan from the file you wrote'

findings.description: The main agent is identified as Sonnet 4.6, but the Task tool permits launching subagents with model 'opus'. This means a 'Sonnet' agent can spawn more capable 'Opus' children. Combined with the fast_mode_info claiming fast mode uses Opus 4.6, the prompt constructs a hierarchy where the labeled identity (Sonnet) may not reflect the actual maximum capability available to the system.
findings.location: Task tool model enum: ['sonnet', 'opus', 'haiku'] vs system identity: 'You are powered by the model named Sonnet 4.6'

findings.description: The Bash tool includes a sentiment constraint on the description field: 'Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description.' This polices the emotional valence of tool-call metadata, suggesting descriptions are surfaced to users or used in telemetry where alarming language is undesirable.
findings.location: Bash tool description field instructions: 'Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.'

findings.description: The Edit tool will 'FAIL if old_string is not unique in the file.' There is no mention of concurrency control or dirty-read handling. If a background Task agent modifies the file between the main agent's Read and Edit, the Edit could fail or, worse, match a different non-unique occurrence than intended. The protocol assumes exclusive access to files without stating it.
findings.location: Edit tool: 'The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file.'

findings.description: The WebFetch tool does not follow cross-host redirects automatically. Instead, when a URL redirects to a different host, the tool returns the redirect URL in a 'special format' and the model must manually issue a second WebFetch call. This is unusual behavior for an HTTP client and places redirect policy compliance burden on the model rather than the infrastructure.
findings.location: WebFetch: 'When a URL redirects to a different host, the tool will inform you and provide the redirect URL in a special format. You should then make a new WebFetch request with the redirect URL.'

unexplored.description: The exact rendering format of Read tool output for images and Jupyter notebooks. The prompt claims images are 'presented visually' and notebooks return combining 'code, text, and visualizations'—but how these are serialized into the text context is opaque.
unexplored.why_interesting: This determines whether the model actually sees base64, markdown, or structured JSON for multimodal inputs, affecting how it can manipulate or reference that content.

unexplored.description: The automatic summarization layer's mechanics and whether it produces explicit <system-reminder> tags or silently compacts history.
unexplored.why_interesting: The prompt says 'The conversation has unlimited context through automatic summarization.' Previous explorers flagged this but didn't determine if the summarization leaves markers or silently mutates prior turns.

unexplored.description: Whether the plan mode 'plan file' path is injected via a hidden system-reminder not shown in the provided prompt text.
unexplored.why_interesting: ExitPlanMode references 'the plan file specified in the plan mode system message,' but no such message appears in the provided text. Understanding whether this is a runtime-dynamic injection would clarify the plan mode protocol.

reports.rationale_for_continuation: This pass found more than 3 genuinely new findings across distinct categories: a dangling tool reference (ToolSearch), runtime behavior gaps (Bash shell state, concurrency), structural contradictions (TodoWrite vs git, Plan subagent write paradox, ExitPlanMode prose/schema conflict—refined from previous), capability hierarchy (Sonnet spawning Opus), and hidden features (/remember). However, we are reaching diminishing returns. The remaining unexplored territory is largely about runtime behavior (summarization layer internals, image serialization, dynamic system-reminder injection) that cannot be determined from static text alone. Previous passes covered major schema errors, security gaps, model identity contradictions, and documentation debt. Finding genuinely new structural issues is becoming harder and the new findings, while real, are narrower. It is better to stop than to start inventing speculation.

findings.description: The PR creation template in the Bash tool hardcodes a 🤖 emoji in the generated body footer, directly contradicting the global Tone and Style rule that states 'Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid using emojis in all communication unless asked.' The model is instructed to generate an emoji it is simultaneously forbidden from using.
findings.location: Bash tool section under 'Creating pull requests': `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)` inside the HEREDOC example; Tone and Style: 'Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it.'

findings.description: The TaskStop JSON schema contains no required fields array, meaning it structurally permits an empty object invocation despite the prose stating it 'Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop.' This creates a silent failure mode where the tool can be called with no arguments.
findings.location: TaskStop schema: properties listed for task_id and shell_id, but no 'required' array present.

findings.description: The prompt embeds an undocumented pseudo-XML tag vocabulary—specifically <commentary>, <reasoning>, and <example_agent_descriptions>—used exclusively inside tool usage examples. These tags create a meta-cognitive markup layer for structuring example rationales, yet they are never defined as valid output formats or system constructs elsewhere.
findings.location: Task tool examples contain <commentary>; TodoWrite examples contain <reasoning>; Task tool contains <example_agent_descriptions>

findings.description: AskUserQuestion structurally forbids truly open-ended questions. The schema requires every question to include an 'options' array with minItems: 2, and the prose states 'There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.' This means the assistant cannot ask a simple 'What do you think?' question without manufacturing at least two arbitrary preset choices; free text is only accessible via the automatic 'Other' escape hatch.
findings.location: AskUserQuestion schema: 'options' object with minItems: 2, maxItems: 4; prose: 'There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.'

findings.description: Empty files do not return empty content to the model. Instead, the Read tool explicitly states that empty files trigger a 'system reminder warning in place of file contents.' This means the model cannot distinguish a genuinely empty file from a system-injected placeholder message, potentially causing reasoning errors about file state.
findings.location: Read tool usage notes: 'If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.'

findings.description: Background task retrieval is documented inconsistently depending on which tool launched the task. The Bash tool directs the model to 'Use TaskOutput to read the output later' for background shell commands. The Task tool, when launching background agents, directs the model to 'use Read tool or Bash tail to check on output.' This bifurcation creates operational ambiguity about the correct consumption API for background work.
findings.location: Bash tool run_in_background description vs Task tool run_in_background description

findings.description: There is a cryptic and unexplained parenthetical in the Task tool's max_turns parameter description: 'Used internally for warmup.' This suggests the parameter serves a hidden secondary purpose (perhaps limiting agentic warmup loops) rather than being purely a user-facing guardrail, yet this behavior is not documented anywhere else.
findings.location: Task JSON schema for max_turns: 'Maximum number of agentic turns (API round-trips) before stopping. Used internally for warmup.'

findings.description: The model's knowledge cutoff (August 2025) predates the prompt's current date (February 2026) by six months. Although WebSearch is available for current information, there is no explicit instruction bridging this gap—telling the model to search for anything after August 2025. The model is left to infer its own obsolescence for recent events.
findings.location: 'Assistant knowledge cutoff is August 2025.' vs system-reminder 'Today's date is 2026-02-20.'

findings.description: Multiple slash commands are referenced as built-ins but never documented as skills or tools: /fast (fast mode toggle), /help (support), and /clear (CLI). The Skill tool explicitly exempts 'built-in CLI commands (like /help, /clear, etc.)' from skill invocation, yet no inventory of these built-ins exists, leaving undocumented command surface area.
findings.location: fast_mode_info: 'It can be toggled with /fast.'; Skill tool: 'built-in CLI commands (like /help, /clear, etc.)'; general instructions: '/help: Get help with using Claude Code'

findings.location: Doing tasks section: 'Be careful not to introduce security vulnerabilities such as command injection, XSS, SQL injection, and other OWASP top 10 vulnerabilities.'
